Tejas, you look like someone carrying a stone. Is it about your colleague? Then let your Irawati bua tell you something. When I was twenty-two, at the bank in Jabalpur, the man who taught me everything was Prakash. He found me a room, showed me the ledgers, shared his lunch when my salary was late.

One evening I saw him quietly move money from an old widow's dormant account into a suspense entry. Once, then again the next month.

I felt sick, and torn. He had been so good to me. So I went to him first, alone. "Prakash ji, I saw the entries. Please put it right, and tell the manager yourself. I'll wait till Friday."

He begged, then went silent. Friday came and nothing changed. On Monday I went to the branch manager with the dates. It cost me his friendship. But I slept again.

qa.a: He moved money from an old widow's dormant account.

qa.a: Young Irawati felt sick and torn, because the man doing wrong had been so good to her.

qa.a: Irawati gave Prakash a chance to correct it by Friday, and when he didn't, she reported it to the manager on Monday.

qa.q: How might Prakash have felt when Irawati confronted him?
qa.a: Prakash likely felt frightened and ashamed, begging and then going silent.

grounding: The elder's story shows a young woman whose wrongdoing colleague was a friend who helped her settle in, giving him a chance to correct it but not staying silent.

The audit was next Wednesday, and Akash knew exactly what the auditors would find. At the pharma warehouse in Baddi, the fridge temperature logs for the vaccine room had been filled in neatly, every two hours, for three weeks, while the fridge was broken. Sumit had written them. Sumit, who had picked Akash up from the bus stand on his first day and found him a room.

Akash spent two nights barely sleeping. On Friday he caught Sumit alone in the loading bay. "I know about the logs. You have to tell Minakshi ma'am before Monday. Those vaccines could be useless."

Sumit's face went white. "You'd do this to me?"

"I'm doing it for the kids who get those vaccines. Monday."

Monday came. Sumit said nothing. At noon Akash knocked on the quality manager's door. Minakshi ma'am listened, pulled the stock aside the same afternoon and called Sumit in.

The owner was in Dubai for a wedding, the health inspector was due tomorrow, and three customers had called in sick after Saturday's biryani. Jahnavi stood by the walk-in fridge in the restaurant kitchen, hand on the door. Its seal had been broken for a month. She had noticed the warm air in the first week and said nothing. It seemed like someone else's job.

Now her stomach churned. If she spoke now, they'd ask why she hadn't earlier. If she stayed quiet, it would only get worse.

She found Uma, the manager, doing accounts. "The walk-in fridge seal is broken. I noticed it weeks ago and didn't report it. I'm sorry. I think it might be linked to the complaints."

Uma stared, then stood. "Show me." They checked the thermometer together. Uma threw out the stock, called a repair man that afternoon and told the owner by phone. "Next time, tell me day one," she said.

In March, Karthik had noticed something odd in the Pune office's billing system: one client was being charged twice for the same server hours. It was a small amount. He meant to mention it. Then the release came, then his leave, and he forgot, or let himself forget.

In September the client's finance team emailed: they had found six months of double charges and were threatening to end the contract.

Karthik read the email three times, his chest tight. He could stay quiet. Nobody knew he had seen it.

That evening he went to his team lead, Nilesh. "I saw this in March and didn't flag it. I should have. Here's what I saw and when."

Nilesh leaned back. "That's not great." A long pause. "But thanks for telling me. Send me your notes. We'll show the client the exact dates." Karthik walked out shaky, and lighter.

qa.a: The client was being charged twice for the same server hours.

Exam week, a power cut, and a phone at eight percent. Jasleen sat on the hostel stairs by candlelight and read the reply to her complaint about the locked fire exit on the third floor: "Noted. Will be looked into." It was the same reply she'd got in August. The door was still chained.

She felt a hard, tired bitterness. Nothing works. Every office is the same. Why bother?

Devika from the student rights group found her there. "Still chained?" Jasleen nodded.

"Then we try another door. The fire department does inspections if residents ask. And the university has a safety committee with student members."

"And if they do nothing too?"

"Then we keep going. Some things take three tries."

After her last exam Jasleen wrote to the fire department, with Devika's group signing too. Two weeks later, an officer visited. The chain came off that afternoon.

qa.a: Jasleen's complaint was about the locked fire exit on the third floor.

qa.a: Jasleen felt bitter and tired, cynical that no office would ever act.

qa.a: Devika suggested other channels, the fire department and the safety committee, and joining others who knew the process, so the problem got real attention.

Gopika had reported the broken drain cover outside the Chennai school gate on the city complaint portal in June. In July, a child fell in up to the knee. In August she reported again and got an automatic message: "Your complaint has been resolved." The drain was still open.

She told everyone at her office tea break: "The whole system is a joke. Nobody is ever going to fix anything. Don't waste your time."

Imran, from accounts, listened. "My residents' association got our streetlights fixed last year. Took them three routes. Want to come to their meeting Saturday?"

She almost said no. She went.

The association knew the ward councillor's office hours, the name of the engineer in charge, and how to escalate a closed complaint. Gopika went with two of them on Monday, with her photos. By Friday a new cover was in place. She still didn't trust the portal. But she trusted people a little more.

At the sugar cooperative in Kolhapur, Uday had told the board that the weighing scale at gate two was rigged, cheating farmers of a few kilos on every cart. The board had started an inquiry. The gate supervisor now looked through him.

But small things happened. On Tuesday someone left a steel tiffin of poha on his desk. On Wednesday Pradeep, who had worked at gate two for ten years, passed him in the yard and said, very low, "Thank you. My father's carts, too." Then walked on quickly.

Uday felt warmth rise in his chest. Courage, maybe. He wished Pradeep would say it at the inquiry. For a moment he almost asked.

Then he thought about Pradeep's three daughters and his loan. He didn't ask. He just nodded. That evening he wrote down the dates of the tiffin and the whisper, not as evidence, but because they kept him going.

qa.a: Uday felt warmed and encouraged, the quiet thanks giving him courage.

qa.a: Pradeep had family and a loan to think of, so accepting his quiet support protected him and avoided making him feel guilty.

qa.q: How might Pradeep see Uday's report?

After Pablo reported to the regional office that the hotel in Seville was making cleaners work unpaid overtime, the manager stopped greeting him. But the notes started.

One on his locker: "Gracias. —a friend." A chocolate bar in his jacket pocket. And one night in the laundry room, Freya, who had been there five years, said without looking up, "You said what we all think. Be careful."

Pablo felt something steady in his chest for the first time in weeks. He also felt a flash of frustration. Why couldn't they say it out loud, at the meeting?

He nearly said it. Then he saw how Freya kept glancing at the door, and remembered she sent money home to her mother.

"Thank you," he said instead. "You don't have to say anything to anyone. I mean that."

Freya looked up, surprised, and her shoulders dropped.

qa.a: It said, "Gracias. —a friend."

qa.q: What was Pablo feeling when the notes and thanks came?
qa.a: Pablo felt steadier and encouraged, though also a flash of frustration that nobody would speak out loud.

qa.q: How did Pablo protect both himself and his colleagues?

Sharmila's new job at the coir board brought her from Kolkata to a small town near Alappuzha, and for the first week she was frightened of everything. She didn't understand Malayalam. She didn't know if she should take off her shoes in the office. At the tea shop she pointed at things and hoped.

On Friday she took off her shoes at the wrong door and a clerk laughed. Her face burned. She wanted to hide in her room and eat instant noodles for a month.

Instead, on Saturday, she knocked on her landlady's door. Avni chechi, who ran the tailoring shop downstairs, explained the rules in a mix of English and gestures, then taught her to say "enthu patti?" for "what happened?"

Sharmila wrote words in a notebook. She watched how people queued at the bus stop. By the next month, she was going to the Sunday market with Avni chechi and her daughters.

Lindiwe laughed with relief. The next week she went with Nadia to a free language café in the library, where people from twenty countries made mistakes together. She kept going to the South African shop on Sundays. But she learned to order bread in German.

Last month, one of the club aunties invited me for Pongal. I cried in the auto on the way home. Not because it fixed everything. Because it was a start.

I'm Kavitha, and moving from Madurai to Delhi for my master's changed small things first. I started wearing jeans to class. I ate at the dhaba with friends, even the chicken. I stopped putting kumkum on in the mornings because I was always late.

Then Appa video-called and saw my bare forehead. He didn't say anything. He didn't need to. I felt like I had betrayed him, and Amma, and Paati who used to braid my hair with jasmine.

For a few weeks I became two people: one on video calls, one in Delhi. It was exhausting.

My brother Shankar told me to just talk. So on the next call I said, "Appa, I still say my prayers. I still speak Tamil with my roommate. Some things I'm changing, some things I'm keeping." Appa was quiet, then said, "Just don't forget where you come from." I won't.

International student advisor's note, Melbourne campus, week 9.

Gopika came to see me for help with her visa forms, but she kept apologising. When I asked what was wrong, she said her mother had seen a photo of her at a friend's birthday, in a short dress, holding a glass of lemonade that looked like wine. Her mother had cried on the phone.

Gopika said, "I feel like I'm betraying them. But I also like who I'm becoming here." She was twisting the strap of her bag.

We talked about how many students feel pulled between two places, and how identity can include both. I suggested she think about what she truly values from home, and what she wants to take from here, and share that with her mother rather than hide.

She wrote a list in my office. She said she'd call her mother that weekend. She'll come back after the visa forms are done.

- Eshaan

Pongal morning in the Hyderabad hostel, and Lakshmi couldn't go home. Her exams started on the fifteenth, the buses were full, and a ticket home cost more than her month's mess bill. She video-called Amma, who held the phone up to the pot boiling over in the courtyard, and everyone shouted "Pongalo Pongal!" Lakshmi smiled until the call ended. Then she locked herself in the bathroom and cried.

It had happened a lot lately. Silent crying in the bathroom, and then telling herself to stop being a baby.

Chandrika from Tirunelveli, two doors down, heard. She knocked. "You too? Come. I have jaggery and rice. The warden let me use the kitchen."

They made sweet pongal on a borrowed stove, badly, laughing. Three other Tamil girls turned up. Afterwards Lakshmi set a reminder: call Amma every Sunday at seven. It still hurt. But it hurt less alone.

In Jyoti's Andheri flat, the fridge held nothing that smelled like home. She missed her mother's fish tenga, the sound of Assamese on the street, her little brother kicking her under the table. Four months into her job, she cried in the shower where her flatmate couldn't hear, then told herself she was weak.

"Me too, for Kolhapur. Here's what helps me. I call home at a fixed time. And I cook one thing from home every Sunday."

Thursday night, Dubai

Amma called today to say that Mausi told the whole family I'm "a manager in a glass tower". I'm Jatin. I'm a junior billing clerk and I share a bunk bed with Lalit in Karama. They want me to send more for Chhotu's college fees, and Papa asked if I can buy the new fridge too.

I didn't correct her. I never do. I just said, "Haan, Amma, all good." Then I sat on the bunk feeling like a fraud, and very far away.

Lalit said his family thinks he's rich too. He said, "Tell them one true thing at a time."

So, plan: Sunday, I'll tell Amma about the bunk bed and the long hours, gently, without complaining. I'll say what I can send and what I can't. It'll hurt her pride. But pretending hurts me more.

qa.q: Where does Jatin share a bunk bed with Lalit?
qa.a: In Karama.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel after saying "all good" to Amma?
qa.a: Jatin felt like a fraud and very far away, lonely in the gap between the story and the truth.

qa.q: What small step does Jatin plan, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Jatin plans to tell Amma one true thing at a time, gently, and say what can and cannot be sent, setting realistic expectations.

qa.q: How might Amma feel on Sunday's call?
qa.a: Amma may feel her pride shaken at first, but also closer to Jatin once she knows the real life behind the story.

grounding: The diary shows a young person whose family boasts about the life abroad and expects money, choosing to share honest difficulties gently rather than pretend.
